`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/WellKnownNames.java:124` is `//			   compilerAlgebra(),` inside `useCompilerLibraries()`, so the compiler world links `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `AnyType` and not `CompilerAlgebra`; the accessor at `:91` and the field at `:40` are live.

`Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss` (29 lines) and `.fsi` (28) declare `AllStandardTotalOrders`, `StandardTotalOrder[\T\]` with `< > <= >= CMP`, and `Equality[\T\] comprises T` with `opr =` defaulting to `===`.

35 test files import it explicitly, and so does `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fsi:13`, so the api is reachable — it is only absent from the *implicit* prelude; `not_working_compiler_tests/MaybeTest15.fss:14` is a file written to use it that does not pass.

Design area: the algebra layer of the compiler prelude, step 2; judgment **finished, unwired** — it is 57 lines of working declarations one uncommented line away from being in every compiled program's prelude, and what that line costs is not measured anywhere.

The tree. `object __DefaultArray2 … mem:PrimitiveArray[\T, (s0 s1) \]` (`FortressLibrary.fss:2420`), `__DefaultMatrix` the same (`:2568`), `__DefaultArray3 … mem:PrimitiveArray[\T,(s0 (s1 s2))\]` (`:2785`). Juxtaposition is multiplication in a static argument: the interpreter evaluates it as `IntBinaryOp` with the operator `" "` (`EvalType.java:461`), and the compiler's mangler spells it `IntBinaryOp` too (`NamingCzar.java:1899-1904`). The plan's `TypeWellFormedChecker` rule rejects any `IntArg` containing `IntBinaryOp` (`nat-checking-plan.md` §c, "What it touches"), so the minimal checker refuses the library's own rank-2 and rank-3 storage. `NatReflect.fss:42-46` (`__refl'[\r+b, b+b\]`) is the fourth site and the design admits that one (§6d).

What follows. Option (c)'s storing objects are rewritten, not copied: a store trait that carries its size as a run-time field instead of `PrimitiveArray[\T,(s0 s1)\]` in the type is what §6d's "the field first" amounts to. That is a departure from the library's text and it is not named as one. The alternative, static arithmetic in the checker, is what the specification marks "not yet supported" (`basic/expressions/constant.tex:15`) and what the team's meeting refused for overloading (`internal-document.tex:167-182`); it is a decision, not a default.

### Serious 6. The array rung of §8 hides three pieces of `.java` work, so the count of gated batches is at least three, not two

The design's count: "First, the checker rung (`.scala`, full gate)… Second, the array rung (`.java`, full gate)" (§8), with a batch holding at most one such rung (§0).

Hidden in the second rung. (a) `CodeGen.java:5784-5792`: an `IntArg` in an `extends` clause throws `CompilerError("Only emitting RTTI for types right now")`; §6a says "every `object … extends Vector[\RR64,s\]` will hit" it, §8's list of the rung's contents omits it. (b) A run-time representation for a nat argument: the loader's generic RTTI class holds one `RTTI` field per static parameter, named `T0…Tn` and typed `RTTI_CONTAINER_DESC` (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:1600-1622`), and the only kind the runtime consults is `opr` (`Naming.java:95-101`, `isOpr`); nothing reads `intnat` (`Naming.java:213` is its only runtime mention). §6d says the stamped class per size is "which the loader already produces from the mangled name (probe 6)"; probe 6 stamped a generic function, which has no RTTI class; a generic object with a nat argument was never stamped (probe 4 died in the checker). (c) The store-selection mechanism of finding 2.

Hidden in the first rung. The plan's "no Java" (`nat-checking-plan.md` §d) is unproven: the object crash's frames are Java (`StaticTypeReplacer.replaceIn:102`, the replacer composition at `:95-99`), six Java files in `compiler/` handle `IntArg` (`TypeDisambiguator.java:402-433`, `TypeNormalizer.java:57`, which synthesises an `IntArg` `"0"` for array types, `StaticTypeReplacer.java`, `NamingCzar.java`, `CodeGen.java`, and the replacer's own test), and the plan's bug (i) says of the source "not identified by reading" (`:492-497`). The design's shadow session (§6e) is the right instrument; its outcome decides whether the checker rung is Scala-only.

Consequence for cost. Checker (`.scala`), then code generator and runtime for nat arguments (`.java`), then store class, trait and factory (`.java`), each in its own batch under the one-Java-rung rule, before `library_tests/Vector1.fss` can pass. Three gated batches at the least; the design says two.

### Serious 7. The unconstrained-nat default is unsafe and does not address what the export checker will actually meet

The design (§7 question 5, default): "default an unconstrained nat to `0`", keeping the library's text at `.fsi:1496-1523`.

What those six declarations are. The api declares `opr +[\T extends Number, nat n, nat m\](me: Vector[\T,n\], other: Vector[\T,n\])` and `-` with a dead `m` (`.fsi:1496-1503`), and the vector products with dead `m, p` (`.fsi:1508-1523`). The component's `+` and `-` are methods of `trait Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]` with one nat (`.fss:2195-2197`), and its products carry one nat `n` (`.fss:2264-2276`). So the api and the component disagree in the number of static parameters, not merely in whether one is constrained. `ExportChecker.equalIntExprs` is `false` with the comment "Not implemented!" (`ExportChecker.scala:645-648`); once it compares, what it compares is a shape mismatch that default-0 at call sites does not touch. The interpreter never runs the export check, which is why the mismatch has lived since 2008.

Why default-0 is the wrong side. A nat left unconstrained by inference and then used as a value in the body (`n.asZZ32`, the spec's "any context a variable of type N32 can appear", `trait-parameters.tex:82-86`) would compute with 0 and no error; the interpreter's analogue, `BottomType` for an unbound parameter (`EvaluatorBase.java:238-240`), errors at first use. The safe rule is the interpreter's: an unsolved nat is an error when it reaches a type, a name or a value, and nothing when it reaches nothing. Whether the six api lines are then edited (a sealed-tree library edit) or the export checker is taught to tolerate a dead parameter is decision E.

### Serious 8. The design gives no stop condition, and the ones `PLAN.md` has do not cover the failures this plan can meet

`PLAN.md`'s stop conditions are a design fork, "a rung's gate red twice after one repair", disk, and a permission wall. None of them fires when the shadow session finds the nat confusion in Java rather than Scala, when the runtime needs a new RTTI kind, when the checker refuses the store selection (finding 2), or when the model cannot be typed without a diff to its text (finding 1). Each of those is a fork returning to Pavol, and the design should say so before the first rung, not after; §7 of this review names five.

### Minor 9. The "unprobed link" of §4c is already proven by the tree, and the rung's first experiment is misdirected

§4c: "Unprobed: that a non-generic trait extending an instantiated generic supertype with a hand-written implementation class compiles and links; it is the first thing the array rung of §8 finds out." `FZZ32 extends fortress.CompilerBuiltin.ZZ32.DefaultTraitMethods implements fortress.CompilerBuiltin.ZZ32` (`FZZ32.java:14-15`) under `trait ZZ32 extends { Number, Equality[\ZZ32\], StandardTotalOrder[\ZZ32\] }` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:210`), and `FJavaString` under `trait JavaString extends String extends StandardTotalOrder[\String\]` (`:25, :52`), are that exact shape and pass the gate every day. Probe `p2_nongeneric.fss` adds the Fortress-object half, reached through the stamped generic `get`: compiles, runs, `p2 5.0`. The first thing the rung should find out is finding 2's question, not this one.

### Minor 10. "The one recorded implementation stance" is a conditional inside a question

§6b reads `internal-document.tex:199-208` as recording "'don't instantiate'" as the team's stance. The text asks whether `f(x: ZZ32)` beside `f(x: T[\0\])` is allowed "if our implementation strategy for nat parameters is 'don't instantiate'?" and answers "Allowed"; two items earlier it allows `T[\1\]` beside `T[\0\]` "now that nat parameters are all instantiated" (`:183-198`). The record is a question under a hypothesis, and the compiled encoding the team then built carries nats by name into instantiations (`MethodMapping.tex:142`, `NamingCzar.java:1891-1911`), which is instantiation. Nothing in the design turns on it, but it is cited as intent.

### Minor 11. What the specification's own breadcrumb on unboxed arrays says, which the design does not cite

Jan's note #82 on unboxed types (`appendices/future.tex:42`): "Do we want to permit arrays of fixed bounds to be unboxed? No. Unboxed arrays are a different other thing. Among other things, an array of fixed bounds may be a segment of another array." That is the team saying that a sized array is a structure (possibly a view) over a linear store and that the store is the thing to unbox, which is the shape of option (c) and of `HeapSequence` (`arrays-distributed.tex:18-22`). It supports the design's separation of sized traits from a native store; it should be in §5.

### Minor 12. Two numbers in §3 are the review's, not the tree's

§3 counts "38 declarations, of which 5 are aliases … 26 are new operations … and 9 are new structures" at `a92569f83`, and says the working copy is "under uncommitted repair"; the brief records that the repair landed as `8590d7a9e`, dropping seven declarations to the library (`array-work-brief.md` §3). The design's counts are of the file before that commit; the current `FlatArrays.fsi` (56 lines) has 31 declarations. Nothing turns on it; the inventory should be re-dated when the design is revised.

## 1b. The design's nat rungs against `reviews/nat-checking-plan.md`

The two documents are the same shape. The plan (2026-09-16) states "nothing was run beyond the probes that already exist" (`nat-checking-plan.md:22-23`); the design (2026-09-19) ran eight probe programs that reproduce symptoms (§9) and compiled no line of any fix. The plan's §f names the directory its prototype would live in, `explorations/perf-probes/nat/`; it does not exist. Its sibling, `template-checking-plan.md` (2026-09-16, "Nothing was run for this document", `:4`), was prototyped the same day under a classpath shadow, 31 changed lines, and gated green with the shadow overlaid (FACTS, the template-checking fix; `perf-probes/template-check/33-testfast.out`, `34-testsystem.out`). So the project has the instrument and the precedent for proving a checker plan before a rung, and the nat plan has not been put through it in four days; the design's §6e re-specifies the same shadow session rather than reporting its result.

Where the design's nat rungs agree with the plan, and simply restate it: the minimal design, symbols and literals unified by equality, no arithmetic (plan §c, design §6b-§6c); the reserved-name `IntRef` for the prototype and the AST node for the real edit (plan §c "Representation", design §6e); the unconstrained nat defaulted to 0 with deletion posed as Pavol's question (plan §c, design §7 question 5); the five nat compiler tests kept green (plan §d, design §6e); shadow first, then the tree (plan §f, design §6e); and the plan's two named bugs outside the checker, the object crash and the `IntArg` in `extends` (plan §c "Two known bugs", design §6a).

Where the design adds to the plan. Probe 4 reduces the object crash to a four-line object with no `extends` and no use of the nat, so it sits on the path of the very first sized declaration, where the plan had it one step later (`pNat2.fss`). Probe 6 finds a defect the plan does not know: a nat in value position types as an integer literal, which the plan lists under "Not touched" as already right (`KindEnv.scala:64-70`), and then compiles to `getstatic NatVal$n.ONLY` and dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError`; the plan's claim is true of the checker and false of the run. Probe 6 also shows the mangler carrying nat literals into instantiation names, which the plan's §g asserts from `NamingCzar.java` and does not run.

Where the two contradict each other, or share one blind spot. (1) Code generation: the plan's §g closes with "if the compiled path ever wants `Vector[\T, n+1\]` the question is codegen's, not the checker's" and its §d says the change "does not by itself flip any catalogued test"; the design folds the code-generator work into the array rung without listing it (finding 6). Neither document owns the `.java` half that the first sized object needs. (2) Applications: the plan's gate step 5 expects `FlatArrays.fss` and `FlatArrays2.fss` to "pass the type checker with no nat-related error" once the minimal design lands (`:586-589`); finding 1 says `FlatArrays.fss:62` cannot, because `reflect(nr)` is statically a `NatParam` and `viewN` takes `N[\r\]`. The plan's §d "covers all 81 and all 30" and the design's §6c "covers all 81 and all of microGPT's" both count declarations; the plan's one worked call site (§b) is `unbox(Box[\3\](7))`, a literal argument, the easy case; neither document types an application whose argument was built at run time, which is every array in the model. (3) The census: the plan's §d table gives 0 for arithmetic inside white brackets in `FortressLibrary.fss` and the design repeats it; `:2420`, `:2568` and `:2785` are arithmetic (finding 5), so the plan's `TypeWellFormedChecker` rule refuses three library objects the design's option (c) needs. (4) The export checker: the plan changes `equalIntExprs` to structural equality (§c "What it touches"); the design says every exported signature mentioning `Vector[\T,n\]` fails today and passes after; neither notices that the six api declarations at `.fsi:1496-1523` do not match the component's shape (finding 7), so the first run of the fixed export checker over the library reports them.

What has been proven by a probe, by either. The symptoms, three times over: probe 11 of the prelude report (`pNat1.fss`, `pNat2.fss`, 2026-09-16), the design's probes 3 to 6 (2026-09-19), and this review's probes for the questions beside the checker (2026-09-20). The fix, nowhere: no edited copy of `Formula.scala`, `TypeAnalyzer.scala` or `STypesUtil.scala` has been compiled by anyone. The plan's size ("about 24 functions in five Scala files, 200-300 lines; no Java", §d) and the design's "one shadow session … then the rung in the tree" (§6e) both rest on the crash being in Scala, which the frames say it is not (finding 6). The one step that changes this is the shadow session, with the plan's four programs plus `NatExtends1` and `NatStore1` from §2 Q3; it is a worker session with no gate, and it should be run before the checker rung is scheduled, not as its first half.

## 2. The seven questions, answered by finding

**Q1, finish or redesign.** It finishes the specification's shape: the sized family `Array k[T, 0, n0, …]` over a generic array (`aggregate.tex:130-136`), both factories (`arrays-distributed.tex:42-48`), a linear store under a structure (`:18-22`, `future.tex:42`), sizes in types (`nutshell.tex:85-86`), and the checker doing what the interpreter's `unifyStaticArg` does (`IntNat.java:127-147`). It departs in six places: the storing objects are rewritten, not copied (finding 5, unnamed); the run-time-sized factory's dynamic half, that an `Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]` is a `Vector` underneath, is dropped (§6d, named as "the one library pattern the compiled world does not reproduce", but its consequence for the model is not, finding 1); natives in place of the team's generated-code unboxing (finding 4, half named); store selection by run-time tag, our roadmap's A2, in place of the team's `Unbox`/expando direction (finding 2, unnamed); a third library text in the compiler world in place of the spec's Core/Standard split and the ruling's "the standard library" (finding 3, unnamed); and the compiler world's own precedent, the unsized rank-polymorphic `ZZ32Vector`, set aside (§4b, named).

**Q2, the defaults.** Finding 2 (store selection: refuted by probe, alternatives all `.java`, precedent points the other way), finding 4 (loops: measured to buy nothing on the model's shapes, no precedent), finding 7 (unconstrained nats: unsafe side, and the real problem is an api/component mismatch). The smaller defaults: the nat also as a run-time field is right and forced (finding 5); the run-time-sized factory returning the unsized `Array` is what breaks the model (finding 1); one shadow session before the checker edit is right and should widen to five probes (§7 below). Which are Pavol's: all three large ones and the run-time-size one; the shadow session is the worker's.

**Q3, the nat plan.** The Scala side is consistent with itself: `staticInstantiation` already substitutes `IntRef` (`STypesUtil.scala:670`), `staticArgsMatchStaticParams` already accepts an `IntArg` for `KindNat` (`:742-747, 767-772`), self-types are built with `IntArg(IntRef)` for nat kinds (`:338-339, 352-353`), and the equality hole is one line (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:332`). Unsound or unproven: the crash is in Java replacer composition (finding 6); "no arithmetic" refuses three library objects (finding 5); the export checker meets an arity mismatch (finding 7); nothing in the plan or the design touches code generation or the runtime for a nat argument, which the first sized object needs (finding 6). Smallest rung that proves or refutes it: the shadow session with `NatInfer1`, `NatObject1`, `NatValue1`, `XXXNatMismatch1` as the design lists them, plus `NatExtends1` (`object V[\nat n\]() extends S[\n\] end` instantiated as `V[\3\]()`, through code generation and a run) and `NatStore1` (a generic factory returning a monomorphic object, the probe `p1_monostore.fss` as it stands). Dead ends: the `TypeArg`/`IntArg` confusion pervasive in the Java front end; a nat needing a runtime RTTI kind; the checker refusing the library's own storing objects with no arithmetic rule the spec permits.

**Q4, `double[]` under the generic trait.** Stamping cannot produce a `[D` field; the design's probe 1 settles that and the map already said it (`map/README.md:43`). The `ZZ32Vector` precedent proves that a hand-written class can implement a trait's `DefaultTraitMethods`, be a `NamingCzar` special type, and reach Java natives through `import java`, and `FZZ32` proves it under instantiated generic supertraits (finding 9). It does not prove unboxed traffic (probe 2, and `KDotStore`), per-instantiation representation, or anything about nats. The route the design proposes for selecting the store is refused by the checker (finding 2); the route that could give unboxed storage per element type under one generic trait is the loader/code-generator one, which `PLAN.md` step 5 says to probe first and which the design dismissed unprobed.

**Q5, the two preludes.** The compiler world, said in §4c and §7's last paragraph, and no more than said: what it costs (a second algebra, ~1,200 lines of array text, two library texts from then on, the interpreter's copy never checked) and what it forecloses (the library route, a reserved fork) are absent (finding 3).

**Q6, the 26 operations and the three kernels.** As written, none is reachable from the model's text and none of the kernels compiles, for the reason of finding 1; the first failure is `FlatArrays.fss:62`, the second `MicroGptFlat.fss:27`. On values that are statically sized (literal sizes, `vector[\RR64,16\]()`), the design serves: the 14 elementwise maps (declared over `Array[\RR64,I\]`, bodies boxed per element under the question-3 default), the library's products and `Diag`, `transpose` of a `Matrix`. It cannot serve as written: `view`, `row`, `row3`, `heads`, `unheads`, `plane` (run-time shapes through `reflect`), `rows` in all four shapes (takes `Matrix`, returns `Array`, so one `rows` cannot feed the next), `gather`, `pick`, `onehot` where the argument is a view's result, and the batched product on `heads`' results. The kernels: `kdot` and `kmat` need `vec`/`mat` to return sized types or `DOT`/juxtaposition to be declared over `Array`; `krows` needs both and `rows`.

**Q7, order and stop.** The first gated rung should not be the checker rung until a shadow rung with no gate has answered five questions (§7 below); the checker rung is right as the first gated rung only if the shadow says the crash is in Scala. The stop conditions are in §7.

off the base `49ee5e91` (R1, R2, the review's corrections, the ladder-criterion wording, the

# The two worlds: separable, with two named exceptions

## Verdict

**Clean with two named exceptions.** No route was found by which an edit confined to `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`/`.fsi`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`/`.fsi`, `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`/`.fsi` and `Library/CompilerSystem.fss`/`.fsi` can change the result of any test `ant testSystem` runs, and the two ways it could are both mechanically checkable before the batch is written.

The exceptions are: (a) **adding or renaming a top-level file** in `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, because both directories are on the interpreter's source path too and resolution is by file name (`useful/Path.java:107-122`, `default_repository/configuration:44`); (b) touching `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss`/`.fsi`, which is in both worlds' root list and is therefore global (`compiler/WellKnownNames.java:48-49,121-126`).

## The rule a batch planner can apply

A batch may drop `ant testSystem` if and only if all four of these hold, each checkable from `git diff --name-only` plus one grep:

1. Every changed, added or deleted path is one of the eight files named above — no `.java`, no `.scala`, no `build.xml`, no `default_repository/configuration`, no `bin/`.
2. No file is added to or removed from `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, and no top-level declaration is renamed in a way that changes an api or component name.
3. `AnyType.fss` and `AnyType.fsi` are untouched.
4. `grep -rl 'CompilerLibrary\|CompilerBuiltin\|CompilerAlgebra\|CompilerSystem\|GeneratorLibrary' ProjectFortress/tests/` is still empty — it is empty today, and it is the one-line restatement of the whole argument.

Any batch that fails one of the four runs the full pair. Test files added under `ProjectFortress/library_tests/` — which every rung of the last climb added — do not break the rule: `library_tests` is read only by `LibraryJUTest`, inside `testFast` (`build.xml` track `library`, `tests/unit_tests/LibraryJUTest.java:36-41`).

The saving is what `iteration-cost.md:68` measured: a median `ant testSystem` of 147.6 s over 11 runs, quoted as 147.5 s at `iteration-cost.md:80,124`.

---

## 1. What the interpreter loads as its prelude, and where the list is

The list is one Java array, `WellKnownNames._defaultLibrary`, initialised at `compiler/WellKnownNames.java:48-49` to `{ anyTypeLibrary(), fortressLibrary(), fortressBuiltin() }`, that is `AnyType`, `FortressLibrary`, `FortressBuiltin`.

`WellKnownNames.useCompilerLibraries()` (`:113-126`) repoints `_fortressLibrary` to `"CompilerLibrary"` and `_fortressBuiltin` to `"CompilerBuiltin"` and rewrites the array to `{ CompilerLibrary, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerAlgebra, AnyType }`; `useFortressLibraries()` (`:128-138`) restores the interpreter's three.

That array is the *only* way the prelude enters a run: `GraphRepository.roots()` returns `defaultLibrary()` verbatim (`repository/GraphRepository.java:125-127`) and `addRoots()` (`:133-165`) makes one graph node per name, resolving each name to a file with `getApiFile` → `findFile(name + ".fsi")` (`GraphRepository.java:390-400`, `useful/Path.java:107-122`).

Resolution is by name against the ordered source path `.` , `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, `Library`, `ProjectFortress/test_library` (`default_repository/configuration:44`); no directory is scanned, no file is opened that a name did not ask for. This is why `Library/` holding both preludes side by side is harmless: the separation is by file name, not by directory.

**Yes, one path loads CompilerLibrary and CompilerBuiltin into the interpreter**, and it is worth writing down because it is the obvious counterexample: `fortress walk -compiler-lib <file>.fss` calls `WellKnownNames.useCompilerLibraries()` and `Types.useCompilerLibraries()` inside the `walk` arm (`Shell.java:1107-1110`; the same flag exists on `disambiguate`/`desugar`/`grammar`/`typecheck` at `Shell.java:860-863`, and it is documented in the usage text at `Shell.java:149,198`).

Nothing under `ProjectFortress/tests/` and nothing in the JUnit harnesses passes `-compiler-lib`; a grep for the flag over the tree outside `.git`, `build/` and `explorations/` matches only `Shell.java` itself. The `testSystem` tests never go through `Shell.subMain` at all (section 3), so they cannot reach the flag even in principle.

The library world is **static mutable JVM state**, so the argument depends on nothing in a `testSystem` JVM ever calling `useCompilerLibraries()`. Every caller is an arm of `Shell.subMain` or a flag parse (`Shell.java:404,411,416,426,429,432,435,438,442,449,454,460,485,490,861,1108`); `SystemJUTest` and `FileTests` call none of them, and `build.xml:1197-1199` gives the shard's `<batchtest>` a fileset of `**/SystemJUTest.class` only, so no compiler test shares the JVM.

## 2. AnyType

`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss` is seventeen lines: `native component AnyType`, `export AnyType`, `trait Any end`. The api `AnyType.fsi` is the same trait.

It is shared, and the map is right to call it so: it is in the interpreter's root list at `WellKnownNames.java:48-49` and in the compiler's at `:121-126`, and `compiler/disambiguator/TopLevelEnv.java:970-972` implicitly imports it into every component in both worlds ("For now AnyType needs to be implicitly imported").

An edit to `AnyType` is therefore global by construction and is excluded from the rule above. It is also the one file whose analysis cache entry collides across worlds — the cache file name is the api name plus a hash of its *source directory*, not its content (`compiler/NamingCzar.java:244-254`), and `AnyType` has one name and one directory in both worlds, so `AnyType-<hash>.tfi` is written by whichever world ran last. Under `testSystem` that channel is closed by a fresh per-shard cache (section 4, route D), but it is the reason `AnyType` is named as an exception rather than argued about.

`CompilerSystem` is in neither root list; it is imported explicitly by the programs that want it (`Library/CompilerSystem.fss:13` imports only `nativeHelpers.systemOps`). It is the safest of the four compiler-world files, not the most dangerous.

## 3. What `ant testSystem` runs, and against which library

`testSystem` (`build.xml:1199-1210`) deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches`, then runs four `systemShard` macros (`build.xml:1167-1196`) in parallel. Each shard forks a JVM whose `<batchtest>` fileset is `**/SystemJUTest.class` and nothing else, with `fortress.suite.shard=i/4`, `fortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES` pointed at `ProjectFortress/test-caches/system-<i>`, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, and `java.io.tmpdir` inside `ProjectFortress/test-tmp`.

`SystemJUTest.suite` (`SystemJUTest.java:29-43`) sets `PhaseOrder.interpreterPhaseOrder` and `setCompiledExprDesugaring(false)`, then returns `FileTests.interpreterSuite(ProjectProperties.BASEDIR + "tests", …)`. It does **not** call `useInterpreterLibraries()`; it relies on the static default of `WellKnownNames.java:48-49`, which is the interpreter triple. That is sound here only because nothing in the shard JVM flips it (section 1), and it is the single most fragile step in the whole argument.

`interpreterSuite` (`FileTests.java:762-846`) walks the top level of `ProjectFortress/tests/` and makes one `InterpreterTest` per `.fss` (`:816-823`) and one `ShellTest` per `.sh` (`:820-823`). That is the 382: 381 `.fss` plus `concurrentPrinting.sh`, matching `map/test-coverage.md` A.3.

`InterpreterTest.justTheTest` (`FileTests.java:712-740`) is in-process: `Shell.setScala(false)`, then `Shell.specificInterpreterRepository(ProjectProperties.SOURCE_PATH.prepend(path))` (`:717`), then `getLinkedComponent` and `Driver.runProgram`. The library the programs link against is therefore exactly the graph roots of section 1 — `AnyType`, `FortressLibrary`, `FortressBuiltin` — plus whatever the program imports by name.

Experiment: a shadow prototype that instantiates one generic class two ways with different backing fields and loads both in one JVM, read against `InstantiatingClassloader.java:178` and the `if (false) { // Here will go all the magic expando-stuff. }` at `:168-172`.

## 3. What design work must come first

### 3a. The sequential piece: the array-representation fork

This is Pavol's and it gates the largest block of value, so what follows is what a sketch would have to contain for him to decide it, not a recommendation.

**What it decides.** Whether an `Array[\RR64,…\]` on the compiled path is backed by boxed elements or by a primitive `double[]`. It is decided by the type's declaration and its natives (`map/README.md` §5 step 2), which is why it cannot be postponed past the declaration: doing step 2 boxed and step 4 unboxed is the same library written twice.

**What is already measured, and is not in dispute.** Over the runtime's own box shape, boxing costs **6.3× on a 4192-element dot product, 6.5× on a 16×16 matrix product and 2.6× on the `rmsn` row lift** against primitive `double[]`, and the generic array object — `Object[]` behind an interface with a `checkcast` per read — adds only **9 %, 1.6 % and 4.8 %** on top (ledger 306). So the cost is the element boxes, not the genericity of the container; that distinction is the useful one for this fork and it is already paid for.

**Three concrete shapes, with what each costs.**

*Shape 1, generic and boxed:* `Array[\T, nat n\]` over `Object[]`, the interpreter's `ImmutableArray` design ported. It reuses the interpreter's library text, it is the only shape that makes the library route (the interpreter's collections as prelude) coherent, and it is the shape the 104 blocked files are written against. It needs `nat` checking (PLAN step 4) before it can be declared. It keeps the 6.3–6.5× measured above and defers unboxing to a rewrite.

*Shape 2, monomorphic and unboxed:* one non-generic trait per element type, which is **what the 2012 team actually shipped in this world**. `trait ZZ32Vector` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:532-549`) is backed by `int[]` in `compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32Vector.java`, with natives in `nativeHelpers/simpleIntVector.java`, an elementwise operator vocabulary in `CompilerLibrary.fss:484-535` (`PREFIX_SUM`, `+`, `-`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `makeZZ32Vector` over `Range`), a `NamingCzar` binding at `:203,337,382,461,553`, and two live tests, `other_compiler_tests/VectorTest2.fss` and `VectorTest3.fss`. An `RR64Vector` by analogy needs no `nat` checking at all — `ZZ32Vector` carries no static parameters — and would be unboxed from the first line. Its cost is that it is a type per element type with no generic code above it, and that **the target program is not written that way**: `explorations/apl/mg/FlatArrays2.fsi` declares its whole vocabulary over `Vector[\T,s\]`, `Matrix[\T,n,d\]`, `Array3[\T,0,p,0,n,0,d\]` with shared `nat` dimensions (`:58-146`), so shape 2 means either rewriting the target program's api or accepting a second spelling beside it.

*Shape 3, generic type with a specialized representation:* `Array[\T, nat n\]` whose class-load instantiation picks a `double[]` backing, which is `performance-roadmap.md` A2. The obstacle is stated in the map's twelve facts: generics are stamped out by **name rewriting** in `InstantiatingClassloader` at class-load time, and "instantiation renames, it does not change representation" (`map/README.md` §2, `modules-and-phases.md` B.11). Whether the loader can be made to select a different backing per instantiation, and what that costs, is the single largest missing piece of evidence in this fork.

**What evidence is missing, and it is little.** One: whether `InstantiatingClassloader` can select a representation per instantiation at all, which decides whether shape 3 exists. Two: what an `RR64Vector` built on the `ZZ32Vector` precedent actually costs to write and whether the three kernels of `perf-probes/kernels/` run on it — that is a measurement, not an argument, and it would put a real number beside shape 2. Three: whether `nat` checking (PLAN step 4) lands cleanly, because shapes 1 and 3 both wait on it and shape 2 does not. §6 gives each of these as one experiment.

**What is not missing.** The performance numbers (ledger 306), the target program's spelling (`FlatArrays2.fsi`), the team's own precedent (`ZZ32Vector` and its five wiring sites), the design intent that sizes live in types on purpose (`preliminaries/intro/nutshell.tex:85-86`, cited in `map/README.md` §5 step 1). A sketch that assembled these four beside the three shapes would be enough to decide on, and it is a worker-sized piece of writing with one probe attached.

**The fork stays open here.** Naming three shapes is not choosing one, and the second reserved fork — the library route, the interpreter's collections as prelude against growing the compiler library — is entangled with it: shape 1 makes the library route coherent and shape 2 does not, so whoever decides the representation is also constraining that.

### 3b. The one piece that can start before the fork

`nat` static parameters in the checker, PLAN step 4. `reviews/nat-checking-plan.md` exists, the symptom is ledger 307 (`STypesUtil.makeInferenceArg` calls `NI.nyi()` for `KindNat`; a written-out `nat` is a `ClassCastException: VarType cannot be cast to IntExpr`), the visible cost today is the three-file `VarType` crash plus `Matrix[\T, nat s0, nat s1\]` being the compiler prelude's only `nat` declaration (`CompilerLibrary.fsi:267`), and **nothing in it depends on whether an array is boxed**.

If one piece of work larger than a batch is wanted that is not blocked on a fork, that is it. The route on record is shadow first (`perf-probes/template-check/run-all.sh`), then the sealed tree.

### 3c. Design a rung can carry on its own

Four decisions belong inside their rung and do not need to precede the climb, provided the rung states them under the provenance block of §4 and the skeptic checks them.

**The `Maybe` spelling.** The 2012 team's own compiler-world draft, commented at `CompilerLibrary.fsi:217-229` and mirrored in `Specification/library/apis/CompilerLibrary.tex:196-206`, spells the empty case `NothingObject[\T\]` with a separate unparameterised `object Nothing` for `coerce`; the interpreter, the spec's `FortressLibrary` and every test in the corpus write `Nothing[\T\]`. Both spellings cannot coexist. Following the team's draft or the corpus is a choice the rung must argue.

**The `Char` naming.** Rename `Character` to `Char` through the prelude and the three `NamingCzar` sites, which is the spec's spelling (`Specification/library/apis/FortressBuiltin.tex:204`) and costs a `.java` edit; or declare `trait Char` with `Character extends Char`, which is library-only but leaves `opr =(self, other:Char)` undeclared so the comparison half of `CharacterTest.fss` still fails; or record the divergence and mark the six files out of reach.

**The diagnostics semantics.** The interpreter's `printThreadInfo` prints the interpreter evaluator's own task state; the compiled world's tasks are the independent implementation in `runtimeSystem/`. Whether the compiler-side function prints the `runtimeSystem` task or merely the JVM thread is small and real, and the three tests only check that it does not fail.

**The failure-mode question**, already standing in `batched-climb-plan.md` §3: where a rung replaces a throwing stub with a computed value, the skeptic establishes what that value is and runs it against the spec.

What does **not** belong inside a rung, and should not be allowed to be decided there: the `Range` static parameter (it changes a declared type the prelude already has and cascades into `IndexOutOfBounds`), and the eight shadowing files of §1c (a semantics question against `declarations.tex`).

## 5. The answer

Nothing in `FortressLibrary.fss` is written for the interpreter's *evaluation*
strategy. 95.3% of it is plain Fortress that the bytecode compiler would be
happy to compile. What is specific to bytecode generation is the 4.7% of native
bindings — and even those are mostly already ported, on the Java side, in
`nativeHelpers/`.

What breaks, and when:

1. **Nothing at DISAMBIGUATE**, once `FortressLibrary` is the prelude rather
   than a component competing with `CompilerBuiltin`. (Compiled as an ordinary
   component it produces 1,417 disambiguation errors, 78% of them the two
   preludes colliding — a red herring.)
2. **92 errors at TYPECHECK**, in the library's *apis*, before the component is
   opened: 62 of them the `comprises`/exclusion rules rejecting the numeric and
   comparison tower (`TotalComparison`, `QQ`, `AnyIntegral`, `Integral[\I\]`,
   `ZZ`/`ZZ32`/`ZZ64`/`NN64`, `AnyMaybe`), 26 of them `Integral[\I\]` bounds
   that the range library does not satisfy. The 2012 team never saw these
   because `walk` sets `fortress.compile.typecheck` false and `StaticChecker`
   returns the tree untouched.
3. **A hard crash at TYPECHECK**, `java.lang.Error: Not yet implemented`,
   whenever a `nat`-kinded static parameter has to be inferred — and a
   different crash (`ClassCastException: VarType cannot be cast to IntExpr`)
   when one is given explicitly. Reproduced in six lines with the compiler's
   own prelude. 81 declarations in `FortressLibrary.fss` and 58 in its api
   carry such a parameter; `CompilerBuiltin.fss` carries none and
   `CompilerLibrary.fss` carries one, declared empty.
4. **DESUGAR and CODEGEN: untested.** Nothing got that far.

Therefore "use `FortressLibrary` for the compiler too" is **not** a port of 108
native bindings plus a handful of checker complaints. It is three things, in
this order:

* implement `nat`/`int` static parameters in the Scala type checker
  (`STypesUtil.makeInferenceArg` and the `StaticTypeReplacer` path behind
  `pNat2`) — or rewrite the library to avoid them, which means giving up
  `Vector[\T,nat s\]`, `Matrix[\T,nat r,nat c\]` and `Array1..3`, i.e. the
  array vocabulary the whole exercise wants;
* fix, or relax, 92 type errors in a hierarchy that has never been checked —
  a language-design conversation about `comprises` and exclusion, not a typo
  hunt;
* then port the 108 native bindings, ~79 of which already have a Java
  counterpart in `nativeHelpers/`.

And only then would we learn what DESUGAR and CODEGEN make of it.

\chaplabel{library-structure}

The Fortress libraries are divided into two basic categories.  The
first, covered in \chapref{default-libraries}, are the libraries that
are automatically imported by every Fortress component and API,
chiefly \TYP{FortressLibrary} and \TYP{FortressBuiltin}.  These
libraries provide the basic numeric types, generators, arrays,
booleans, exceptions, and the like.  The second, covered in
\chapref{optional-libraries}, are libraries that must be explicitly
imported by the programmer.  These include \TYP{List}, \TYP{Set}, and
...
Two sets of libraries are imported into every Fortress program by
default.  The first, \TYP{FortressLibrary} (\secref{FortressLibrary}),
implements the high-level functionality that will be used by most
Fortress programmers.  It will eventually be possible to selectively
exclude portions of this library from a component if desired.  By
contrast, the second set of libraries are the \emph{builtins}
(\secref{builtins}).  These libraries are intended to encompass
primitive functionality that must be visible in every Fortress
component.

Third, library-only rungs: `Array2`, `Matrix`, the transposed views and the shared-nat products (`kmat` timed); `Array3`; the scalar extension and elementwise maps for `RR64` arrays in the `ZZ32` block's style, which is where the compile path's overloading check on the model's operator pairs is measured; `Char` (5 components) and the immutable variant (`ImmutableArray`, 3 components and 26 ladder files) in whichever order the counts rank them.

## 9. The probes behind §2 and §6 (2026-09-19, private cache, nothing committed)

The compiler world's library was compiled into a private `FORTRESS_CACHES` in the order of `repo-internals.md:170-179` (five components, all exit 0), and each probe was `fortress compile` then `fortress run` from the scratchpad.

Probe 1, stamping. `object Box[\T\](x: T) getter get(): T = x end` with `Box[\RR64\](1.5)` and `Box[\ZZ32\](3)`; prints `4.0` and `4`. The jar holds the template `GenBox$Box⟦⟧.class`, whose `javap -p` shows `Field "\%x":LT;` and `public T get()`. Run with `-Dfortress.bytecodes.expanded.directory` set, the loader saved the stamped `GenBox$Box⟦…FRR64⟧.class`, whose field is `Lcom/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FRR64;` and whose `get` returns `FRR64`. content.content:
\TYP{Any} comprises of tuple types, arrow types, \TYP{()}, and \TYP{Object}.

The exclusion relation is a symmetric relation between two types
whose intersection is \TYP{BottomType}.
Because \TYP{BottomType} is uninhabited
(i.e., no value has type \TYP{BottomType}),
types that exclude each other are disjoint:
no value can have a type that is a subtype of two types that exclude each other.
\note{
The converse is technically not true: we can define two traits with
 method declarations
 such that no trait or object can extend them both, so no value can have a
 type that is
 a subtype of both trait types, but the trait types do not exclude each
 other.  For example:
 trait A f(self, y: Object) = 1; end
 trait B f(x: Object, self) = 2; end
 trait C f() = 3; end

No pair of the three trait types defined above can be extended
but none of them exclude any of the others.
}
Note that \TYP{BottomType} excludes every type including itself
(because the intersection of \TYP{BottomType} and any type is \TYP{BottomType}),
and also that no type other than \TYP{BottomType} excludes \TYP{Any}
(because the intersection of any type $T$ and \TYP{Any} is $T$).
\TYP{BottomType} is the only type that excludes itself.
Also note that if two types exclude each other
then any subtypes of these types also exclude each other.


----
(described in \chapref{traits} and \chapref{objects}).
A trait has a \emph{trait type} of the same name.}

A trait type is a subtype of every type
that appears in the \KWD{extends} clause of its definition.
In addition, every trait type is a subtype of \TYP{Any}.

A trait declaration may also include an \KWD{excludes} clause,
in which case the defined trait type
excludes every type that appears in that clause.
Every trait type also excludes every arrow type and every tuple type,
and the special types \TYP{()} and \TYP{BottomType}.

\subsection{Object Trait Types}
\seclabel{object-traits}

An object trait type is a trait type defined by an object declaration.
Object declarations do not include \KWD{excludes} clauses,
but an object trait type cannot be extended.
Thus, an object trait type excludes any type that is not its supertype.

\KWD{where} clauses.

Trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of
themselves. For example, we can write:
%trait C[\S\] extends C[\T\]
%  where {S extends T, T extends Object}
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{extends} C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\

# The library route: judgement

Terms. **Prelude**: the apis every program gets without importing them. **World**: a prelude plus the switches that go with it (`Shell.useCompilerLibraries()`); `fortress file.fss` runs the interpreter's world, `fortress compile` the compiler's. **Checker**: the static type checker, which runs only in the compiler's world. **Builtins**: the prelude's lowest layer, where Fortress declarations are bound to Java code (**natives**). **Exclusion**: the rule that two types can share no value, which is what lets the checker refuse a trait that extends both. **`nat`**: a static parameter that is a number, used for array sizes. **Rung**: one edit plus its test under the full gate (median 54 minutes measured). **Gated batch**: up to four rungs under one gate (3 to 5 hours landed, two measured). **Worker session**: one delegated report with its probe, no gate.

## 1. Is there a reason on record to keep a second library?

No. Nothing on record argues for two libraries as a destination, and Pavol's reading is the record's: the split was made on 2008-12-19 as a "stripped-down minimalist … first crack at compilation"; its switch is commented "hopefully temporary hack" in the tree today (`WellKnownNames.java:109-111`); the team called what went into it "bogus" (2009) and "bogo-trait" (June 2012, its last edit); the specification names one default library and never the compiler's (`library/structure.tex:13-22`, `default-libraries.tex:15-24`; no `.tex` in the tree contains the word `CompilerLibrary`). What the team did not leave is a plan for ending it: they grew the copy for three and a half years behind the wall they named at the wind-down, the type system against the JVM. That is a record of what they could do, not a position; overruling it costs nothing.

Each reason the brief and the reviews raise, judged:

- **A place the interpreter cannot see.** True (`next-climb/worlds.md`: an edit confined to the compiler prelude cannot reach the 384 interpreter tests) and never used: every batch gate has run `testSystem` anyway (`climb-batch-workflow.md:44`). Under one library a library edit is checked by both suites, which is the discipline Pavol set, not a loss. Not a reason for two.
- **Two native mechanisms.** Real, and a reason for two *binding* files, not two libraries: 95.3% of `FortressLibrary.fss` is plain Fortress; the natives are 108 bindings there and 231 in `FortressBuiltin.fss`, the builtins layer the specification itself separates from the library. Work before: re-bind those 339 (about 79 of the 108 have a `nativeHelpers` counterpart; the overlap for the 231 is uncounted, and the compiler world's 330 `import java` aliases cover the same types). Whether the builtins are one text with `import java` running on both paths, or one api with a component per path, is decided by one half-session probe nobody has run: `ForeignJava` is wired into the interpreter at `Driver.java:441` and exercised by no test. Not a reason for two.
- **The desugaring settings and the four well-known types.** One setting differs in substance: the compiler world gives an unbounded type parameter an implicit `extends Object`, and the specification says exactly that (`trait-parameters.tex:49-50`), so the compiler's setting is the spec's and the interpreter's is the divergence; the reconciliation keeps the compiler's. The four types (`String`, `JavaString`, `Exception`, `CheckedException`) are placed by `Types.useFortressLibraries()` once the world is one; the cost is the sources that name `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.X` literally (38 Java/Scala files, 21 of them the runtime's value classes such as `FZZ32`, plus the frozen stub `src/fortress/CompilerBuiltin.java`), a rename in the switch-over batch. Not a reason for two.
- **The checker's `nat` gap.** Blocks every route equally, growing the copy included, because the target vocabulary is sized (ruling of 2026-09-19). It is PLAN step 4 under any library. Not a reason for two.
- **The 27 exclusion sites.** The brief says only the `excludes` clause is in the specification. That is not right. The types chapter states three of the checker's four clauses: the `excludes` clause (`types-vals-vars.tex:212-214`), object-ness ("an object trait type excludes any type that is not its supertype", `:222-224`) and propagation to subtypes (`:163-164`). It does not state exclusion derived from `comprises`, and it contradicts the fourth clause: a trait "is allowed to extend other instantiations of itself" (`trait-parameters.tex:339-345`), while the checker's `checkP` (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:446-457`) makes two instantiations of one generic exclude each other, which is the shape of the numeric tower (`ZZ32 extends ZZ64`, both `Integral[\·\]`) and of the two reductions the library itself comments as a "Hack". Which clause fires at which of the 23 remaining sites was not traced. So this is work before, in two parts: trace the clause per site (one worker session), then fix the library where a stated rule fires and the checker where the contradicted one does; a decision reaches Pavol only where the spec is silent, the `comprises` clause. The compiler world avoids this today only by keeping its tower flat (`ZZ32 extends { Number, Equality, StandardTotalOrder }`, no `ZZ64`, no `Integral`), which is the bogo-trait; under the ruling that extensions go into the library "in its own patterns" a copy would grow the tower and meet the same rules. Not a reason for two.

One thing only one library gives: the checker on interpreter programs, which Pavol asked for on 2026-09-15 and which FACTS says means giving the checker the interpreter's prelude. It arrives the day the prelude passes TYPECHECK, before any native is ported.

## 2. The order

Destination: the compiler's prelude is the specification's, `AnyType`, `FortressBuiltin`, `FortressLibrary`, and `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra` are deleted at the switch-over. From `main` at the batch-2 landing:

**Step 0, now: stop adding to the compiler prelude.** Nothing is in flight (the tree is clean; the nine `wip/` remotes are landed batches awaiting deletion). The fourteen fork-free rungs were forecast to move 38 files by one phase and no microGPT component, and every one of them is a declaration `FortressLibrary` already has. Codegen rungs continue, being compiler work under any library: `forTryAtomicExpr` (row 353), `LetFn` (row 304), `ObjectExpr`, the eleven-file array-literal crash at `Misc.scala:876`. Prelude rungs stop: `Char`, `Thread`, `round`/`truncate`, `IndexOutOfBounds`, `abort`/`printThreadInfo` as declarations. The landed rungs' tests stay; the ten `library_tests` files that use compiler-world spellings (`NothingObject`, `Character`, `ZZ32Vector`) are rewritten at step 5.

**Step 1, the first rung: the interpreter prelude through the checker, as a gate stage.** Edit: `fortress typecheck` gets a `-fortress-lib` switch, the mirror of `-compiler-lib` (`Shell.java:860-863`; `typecheck` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` unconditionally today), or the 46-line `perf-probes/prelude/WorldFlip.java` moves into the harness; a stage in `climb-batch-workflow.js` beside the ladder regression runs the checker over the three apis and what they import under a private cache, prints the per-api error table and the crash line, and lands the table as the comparand, as the ladder's phase table is. What it proves: that the distance to one library is measured by every gate from now on, and that the world switch is four lines. Stop condition: two runs print the same table (93 errors, 48 sites, 12 apis, `Not yet implemented` at `STypesUtil.scala:557`); the count is red, the suite is green; no library line changes. This is the one place the test-first rule is met by a stage rather than a `.fss`, because no program can yet be compiled against that prelude; the stage is permanent, which is what the rule protects.

Same batch, rungs 2 and 3, the defects with no question attached: family C, the fifteen `RangeInternals.fsi` bounds (`I extends AnyIntegral` where `Integral[\I\]` is required), 26 errors; families D and F and the site that extends and excludes `Condition[\()\]` in one line (`FortressLibrary.fsi:2526`), 4 errors. Gated by `testSystem`, which runs this code. Expected: 93 → 63 at 23 sites, nothing new. Stop: a fix that would change a declared type rather than a bound.

**Step 2, three worker sessions in parallel, no gate.** (a) The exclusion trace: for each of the 23 sites, which of the four clauses fires, beside the spec lines above; output: the sites under a stated rule (library rungs), the sites under the contradicted clause (a checker rung), and the sites under the `comprises` clause, the only decision that reaches Pavol. (b) The `nat` shadow session the review's decision F specifies: where the crash is (Scala or Java, finding 6), the export checker on the six dead-nat declarations (decision E: E2 in the checker, E3 the six-line api diff shown to Pavol), `NatExtends1`, `NatStore1`, and the loader probe that decides decision A (A2, the team's direction, against A3). (c) The half-session probe: a two-declaration component bound with `import java`, run by the interpreter; decides the builtins' shape for step 5.

**Step 3, the `nat` rung, then the exclusion rungs.** PLAN step 4 in the tree, shadow-proven, `.scala` plus whatever `.java` the shadow found: one to two gated batches. Decision E lands inside it. Then step 2(a)'s rungs, zero to two, or the `comprises` decision first. Stop condition of the phase: the stage prints zero errors and no crash, and `FlatArrays.fsi` type-checks with no error of its own (already true but for `nat`, FACTS). Milestone: `fortress typecheck -fortress-lib` works on interpreter programs.

**Step 4, one worker session: the prelude through DESUGAR and CODEGEN once.** No run has ever reached them with this library; the size is not on record. Output: the hole list, each hole a codegen rung, most of them rungs the ladder needs anyway.

**Step 5, the switch-over: at least two gated batches, with the one-`.java`-rung rule relaxed for them (as B1 proposed for the interpreter batch).** Batch one, the natives, re-bound as 2(c) decided: the 29 of 108 without a helper written, the 231 of `FortressBuiltin` matched to the compiler's helpers. Batch two, the names: the 38 sources and the frozen stub re-pointed; the two `useCompilerLibraries()` collapsed to one world with the extends-`Object` setting kept; the compile recipe's five files made three; the five prelude files deleted; the at least 48 compiler-side tests that name compiler-world spellings (a rough grep) rewritten to the spec's (`Nothing[\T\]`, `Char`). Gate: the full suite, the atomic runs, and the ladder regression, where the 85 passes must hold and the 104 fork-blocked files are expected to move off `Array is undefined`. Not settled: whether `FZZ32` implements `FortressLibrary.ZZ32` or `FortressBuiltin.Int` (the interpreter's `Int` is a value object under the trait; the compiler's value class is the trait's implementation); and, if 2(c) says two components, the mechanism, which is the step row 320 found missing (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`).

**Step 6, decision D: a diff, no code.** The model's static types (D1 with D3, the review's default) shown to Pavol as the diff of `rmsn` and `step`'s signature, as soon as step 3 lands and before any array rung.

**Step 7, the array rungs against the library's existing `Array`, `Vector`, `Matrix`, with no copy to write.** Decision A's `.java` rungs as 2(b) decided, at least three gated batches (finding 6: `IntArg` in `extends` at `CodeGen.java:5784`, a runtime kind for `nat` arguments, the store); then decision B, unboxing by static type in generated code (B2), the largest codegen work in the plan, its first measurement `kdot` compiled over the store against `KDotPrim`. End state: the 31 declarations of `FlatArrays.fsi` type-check and compile against the one library, the model's text as D decided.

## 3. Costs, and what each route forecloses

| step | units |
|---|---|
| 1 | 1 gated batch (3 rungs) |
| 2 | 2 worker sessions + 1 half session |
| 3 | 1–2 gated batches + 0–2 rungs, or 1 decision first |
| 4 | 1 worker session + codegen rungs, count unknown |
| 5 | ≥ 2 gated batches |
| 6 | one diff |
| 7 | ≥ 3 gated batches, then B, unmeasured |

To the point where the prelude is one and the checker passes it: about four to five gated batches and four worker sessions. The array work after it is the same under any route.

Growing the copy to the same target costs the copy itself, the array layer and the algebra above `Number` written a second time (about 1,200 lines plus `AdditiveGroup`, `MultiplicativeRing`, `Indexed`, `ReadableArray`, finding 3), at least three batches of library rungs; plus the same `nat` rung, the same A and B, and the same exclusion rules as the copy's tower grows; and it never gives the checker on interpreter programs. It is cheaper only for the 38 files it can move by one phase.

Forecloses. One library: the compiler world's spellings (`NothingObject`, `Character`, `Option`/`Some`), which the goal already rules against; the never-used sandbox; the 298 lines of revival prelude text, superseded, their tests kept. Two libraries: the checker on interpreter programs; the array vocabulary without a copy; the standard library ever being one thing.

Not settled by the evidence, in the order it is met: whether `import java` runs under the interpreter (2c); which clause fires at each tower site (2a); whether the `nat` crash is in Scala or Java (2b); whether the loader can select a representation (2b); what the library meets in DESUGAR and CODEGEN (4); the overlap of the 231 builtins with the compiler's helpers (5); the size of B (7).

## 4. The decision

What we do: make the specification's default library, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, the compiler's prelude, and delete `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra` when the switch-over lands; from now on no declaration goes into the compiler prelude, and codegen rungs continue.

What it changes: the standard library exists once; every library edit is gated by both suites; the checker becomes usable on interpreter programs when the prelude passes it; the array vocabulary is not written a second time; the thirteen revival commits to the compiler prelude are superseded and their tests kept.

Alternatives: keep growing the copy (reaches no microGPT component, runs out at 38 files, every line a copy to delete later); one text with two binding components for the builtins (a variant of the same destination, chosen by the step 2(c) probe, not by Pavol); both at once (two gates, no gain).

Default: one library, the interpreter's, with the builtins' shape decided by the probe. First rung: the interpreter prelude through the checker as a gate stage (step 1).

input.message:
Delivered `explorations/coordinator/library-route-judgement.md`, commit `6af77573a`, pushed to `main` and `claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8` (main had moved to `a282541d2` meanwhile; committed on top with `--only`).

Q1, one sentence: nothing on record argues for keeping the compiler's second library as a destination; every reason raised (the sandbox, the two native mechanisms, the desugaring settings and well-known types, the nat gap, the 27 exclusion sites) is work before one library can serve both, and the team's three and a half years of growing the copy is a record of what they could do behind the JVM wall, not a position to overrule. One correction to the brief: the spec states three of the checker's four exclusion clauses (`types-vals-vars.tex:163-164, 212-224`) and contradicts the fourth (`trait-parameters.tex:339-345`, a trait may extend other instantiations of itself), which is the tower's shape.

First rung: the interpreter prelude through the checker as a gate stage (a `-fortress-lib` switch on `fortress typecheck`, or the 46-line `WorldFlip.java` moved into the harness); proves the distance is measured by every gate; stop: two runs print the same table (93 errors, 48 sites, the `nat` crash), suite green, no library line changed.

Order:
0. Stop adding to the compiler prelude now (nothing in flight); codegen rungs continue.
1. Batch: the gate stage + families C, D, F and `:2526` (93 -> 63 errors).
2. Three worker sessions in parallel: exclusion trace per site; the nat shadow session (decisions E and A's loader probe inside it); the `import java`-under-the-interpreter probe.
3. The nat rung (1-2 batches, E lands inside), then the exclusion rungs or the one `comprises` decision; milestone: the checker on interpreter programs.
4. One session: the library through DESUGAR and CODEGEN once; hole list.
5. Switch-over, >= 2 batches: 339 natives re-bound, 38 sources and the stub renamed, five prelude files deleted, ~48 tests respelled.
6. Decision D as a diff, no code.
7. Array rungs against the library's existing types: A (>= 3 batches), then B (unmeasured).

Cost to one checked prelude: about 4-5 gated batches + 4 worker sessions; the copy route costs the array layer twice plus the same nat/A/B work and never gives the checker on interpreter programs. Unsettled: the interpreter `import java` probe, per-site clause attribution, nat crash location, loader representation selection, DESUGAR/CODEGEN holes, the 231 builtins' overlap, B's size.

Decision: make `FortressLibrary` + `FortressBuiltin` the compiler's prelude and delete the compiler's three; no new compiler-prelude declarations from now; codegen rungs continue. Alternatives: keep growing the copy; one text with two builtin components (a variant chosen by the probe); both at once. Default: one library, the interpreter's; first rung as above.
